Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah decrees the affairs of this world until the following year on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), whatever occurs of life, death, or provision. Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others said the same. It was also said: except for wretchedness and happiness, for these two do not change. This was reported from Ibn ʿUmar. Al-Mahdawi said: the meaning of this view is that Allah, mighty and majestic, commands the angels concerning what will happen in that year, and this was always in His knowledge, mighty and majestic.

ʿIkrimah said: it is the night of the middle of Shaʿban, in which the matter of the year is finalized, the living are separated from the dead, and the pilgrims are recorded, so that no one is added to them and no one is subtracted from them.

ʿUthman ibn al-Mughirah reported: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Lifespans are decreed from Shaʿban to Shaʿban, to the point that a man marries and has children, though his name has already gone out among the dead." And from the Prophet ﷺ he said: "When it is the night of the middle of Shaʿban, stand in prayer during its night and fast during its day, for Allah descends at sunset to the lowest heaven and says: Is there anyone seeking forgiveness, that I may forgive him? Is there anyone afflicted, that I may heal him? Is there anyone seeking provision, that I may provide for him? Is there anyone who... is there anyone who... until dawn breaks." Mentioned by al-Thaʿlabi.

al-Tirmidhi related with a similar meaning from ʿAʾishah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Allah, mighty and majestic, descends on the night of the middle of Shaʿban to the lowest heaven and forgives more people than the number of hairs of the goats of the tribe of Kalb." There is also a report on this subject from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Abu ʿIsa (al-Tirmidhi) said: We do not know the hadith of ʿAʾishah as a marfuʿ report except through the narration of al-Hajjaj ibn Artah from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir from ʿUrwah from ʿAʾishah. I heard Muhammad (al-Bukhari) weaken this hadith, and he said: Yahya ibn Abi Kathir did not hear from ʿUrwah, and al-Hajjaj ibn Artah did not hear from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir.

I say: The author of the book al-ʿArus has mentioned the hadith of ʿAʾishah at length, and he chose that the night in which every wise matter is distinguished is the night of the middle of Shaʿban, and that it is called the Night of Acquittal (Laylat al-Baraʾah). I have mentioned his view and the refutation of it in another place, and that the correct view is that it is indeed the Night of Power, as we have explained.

Hammad ibn Salamah related: Rabiʿah ibn Kulthum told us: A man asked al-Hasan while I was with him: "O Abu Saʿid, do you think the Night of Power occurs in every Ramadan?" He said: "Yes, by Allah, besides whom there is no god, it occurs in every Ramadan. It is the night in which every wise matter is distinguished; in it Allah decides every creature, lifespan, provision and deed until its like (the following year)."

Ibn ʿAbbas also said: In the Night of Power, from the Mother of the Book is recorded what will happen in the year of death, life, provision, rain, and even the pilgrimage, so it is said: so-and-so will perform the pilgrimage, and so-and-so will perform it. Concerning this verse he said: You see a man walking in the markets while his name has already been written among the dead. This manifestation of the rulings of the year is only for the angels entrusted with the causes of creation. We have already mentioned this meaning above.

al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: The majority of scholars hold that it is the Night of Power. Some said it is the middle night of Shaʿban, and this is false, because Allah, the Exalted, said in His true and decisive Book: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], specifying that the appointed time of its revelation is Ramadan. Then He specified the night here by His saying "in a blessed night." Whoever claims it is in another time has greatly slandered Allah. There is no hadith on the middle night of Shaʿban that can be relied upon, neither concerning its virtue nor concerning the abrogation of lifespans in it, so do not pay attention to it.

al-Zamakhshari: "It was said that the copying of this begins from the Preserved Tablet on the Night of Acquittal, and the completion occurs on the Night of Power. The register of provisions is handed to Mikail, the register of wars to Jibril, and likewise earthquakes, thunderbolts and landslides; the register of deeds to Isma'il, lord of the lowest heaven, who is a great angel; and the register of calamities to the Angel of Death. It is reported from some of them: every worker is given the blessings of his deeds, so that his praise is cast upon the tongues of creatures and awe of him upon their hearts." It is read "nufarriqu" with the doubled letter, and "yafriqu" with each vowelled for the active, with "kullu" in the accusative, and the Distinguisher is Allah, mighty and majestic. Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, read "nufarriqu" with a nun. "Kullu amrin hakim": every matter possessing wisdom, meaning a matter made in accordance with what wisdom requires.

The Almighty's words: ﴿a command from Us﴾. Al-Naqqash said: "The command (al-amr) is the Qur'an, which Allah sent down from Him." Ibn 'Isa said: "It is what Allah decreed on the blessed night concerning the circumstances of His servants." It is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Likewise, ﴿a mercy from your Lord﴾, and according to al-Akhfash these two are both circumstantial qualifiers, the implied sense being: "We sent it down commanding [with it] and showing mercy."

Al-Mubarrad said: "amran" is in the position of a verbal noun, and the implied sense is: "We sent it down as a sending down." Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "amran" is governed by "yufraq" (is decided), like your saying: "yufraqu farqan" (it is decided with a deciding). So "amr" in the sense of "farq" (distinction) is a verbal noun, like your saying: "yadribu darban" (he strikes a striking). It was also said: "yufraqu" indicates "yu'mar" (is commanded), so it is a verbal noun governed by what precedes it.

﴿Indeed We were ever sending [messengers]. A mercy from your Lord﴾. Al-Farra' [the clause "qala al-Farra'" is omitted in one manuscript] said: "rahmatan" is the object of "mursilin" (senders). And the mercy is the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Zajjaj said: "rahmatan" is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), meaning: "We sent him for mercy." It was also said: it is a substitute (badal) for His words "amran." And it was said: it is a verbal noun.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "amran" is put in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas). He made every command majestic and grand by describing it as "hakim" (wise), then increased its grandeur and magnificence by saying: "I mean by this command a command originating from Us, existing from Our presence, and as Our knowledge and management require." In the reading of Zayd ibn 'Ali, "amrun min 'indina" (in the nominative), with the sense "it is a command," and this supports its accusative status as a specification. Al-Hasan read "rahmatun" (in the nominative), with the sense "that is a mercy," and this supports its accusative status as an object of purpose.

The words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾. The Kufans read "rabbi" (Lord) in the genitive (bi-l-jarr). The rest read it in the nominative (bi-l-raf'), as a response to His words "Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." If you wish, it may be read as a nominative beginning (ibtida', a sentence opened with a noun), with the predicate being "there is no god but He." Or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject, with the sense: "He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." The genitive reading is in apposition (badal, substitution) for "your Lord," and likewise "﴿your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old﴾" is read in the genitive in both places. This was transmitted by al-Shaizari [[He is Isa ibn Sulayman Abu Musa al-Hijazi. He was from the Hijaz, then moved to Shaizar (like Haydar, a town near Hama), and remained there until he died, so he was attributed to it. He took the reading from al-Kisa'i both by presentation and by hearing, and he had individual transmissions from him.

(Ghayat al-Nihaya).]] from al-Kisa'i. The rest read it in the nominative as a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a new independent clause). Then this address may be with one who acknowledges that Allah created the heavens and the earth, meaning: if you are certain of Him, then know that He has the right to send messengers and to send down scriptures. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 10–11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾. "Irtaqib" means: wait, O Muhammad, for these disbelievers, for the Day when the sky brings a visible smoke. This was said by Qatadah. It was also said: its meaning is: keep their saying in mind so that you may bear witness against them on the Day when the sky brings a visible smoke, and for this reason the guardian (al-hafiz) is called raqib (watcher).

Regarding the smoke there are three opinions. The first is that it is one of the signs of the Hour which has not yet come, and that it will remain on the earth for forty days, filling what is between the sky and the earth. As for the believer, it will afflict him like a cold (zukam), but as for the disbeliever and the wicked, it will enter their noses, pierce their ears, and constrict their breathing, and it is one of the effects of Hell on the Day of Resurrection. Among those who said that the smoke has not yet come are: Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Amr, Abu Hurairah, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Mulaykah and others.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri related it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report: it is a smoke that agitates people on the Day of Resurrection; the believer will be affected by it like a cold, and it will inflate the disbeliever until it comes out of every opening of his hearing. Al-Mawardi mentioned it.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu al-Tufayl, from Hudhayfah ibn Usayd al-Ghifari, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) looked upon us while we were discussing, and he said: "What are you discussing?" They said: "We are discussing the Hour." He said: "It will not arise until you see before it ten signs," and he mentioned: "the smoke, the Dajjal, the beast, the rising of the sun from its west, the descent of Isa ibn Maryam, the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, three eclipses: an eclipse in the east, an eclipse in the west, and an eclipse in the Arabian Peninsula, and the last of that is a fire that comes out of Yemen and drives people to their gathering place."

In another narration from Hudhayfah: "The Hour will not occur until there are ten signs: an eclipse in the east, an eclipse in the west, an eclipse in the Arabian Peninsula, the smoke, the Dajjal, the beast of the earth, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the rising of the sun from its west, and a fire that comes out from the bottom of Aden, driving people."

Al-Tha'labi also related it from Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first of the signs to emerge will be the Dajjal, the descent of Isa ibn Maryam, and a fire that comes out from the bottom of Aden Abyan, driving people to the gathering place. It spends the night with them wherever they spend the night, it takes its rest with them when they rest, it reaches the morning with them when they reach it, and it reaches the evening with them when they reach it."

I said: "O Prophet of Allah, what is the smoke?" He said: "This is the verse: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾, which fills what is between the east and the west, and remains for forty days and nights. As for the believer, it will afflict him with something like a cold, and as for the disbeliever, he will be like a drunkard; the smoke will come out of his mouth, his nostrils, his eyes, his ears and his rear."

This is one opinion.

The second opinion is that the smoke was what befell the Quraysh of hunger through the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ), to the extent that a man would see between himself and the sky something like smoke. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. He said: Allah has removed it from them, and had it been the Day of Resurrection He would not have removed it from them. The hadith from him with this content is in Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim and al-Tirmidhi. Al-Bukhari said: Yahya narrated to me, he said: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Muslim, from Masruq, who said: Abd Allah said: This only happened because the Quraysh, when they disobeyed the Prophet (ﷺ), he invoked against them with years like the years of Yusuf, so they were struck by drought and hardship until they ate the bones, and a man would look at the sky and see between himself and it something like smoke from hardship. So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke. It will cover the people; this is a painful punishment﴾. He said: Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came and it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, ask Allah for rain for Mudar, for they have perished." He said: "For Mudar? Indeed you are [audacious]!" So he asked for rain and they were given rain, and the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. When they were given ease, they returned to their former state when ease had befallen them, so Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿On the Day We will seize with the greatest seizure; indeed, We will take retribution﴾.

He said: It means the Day of Badr. Abu Ubaydah said: "al-Dukhan" means drought. Al-Qutabi said: It was called smoke because of the dryness of the earth from it, when it rises from the earth like smoke.

The third opinion is that it is the Day of the Conquest of Makkah, when dust veiled the sky. This was said by Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj. "It will cover the people" is in the position of a description of the smoke. If it has already passed, according to what Ibn Mas'ud said, then it is specific to the polytheists of Makkah; and if it is one of the signs of the Hour, then it is general, according to what preceded. "This is a painful punishment" means: Allah says to them: "This is a painful punishment." Whoever says that the smoke has already passed, then His saying "This is a painful punishment" is a narration of a past situation, and whoever makes it future, then it is a narration of a coming situation. It was also said: "This" means "that." It was also said: that is, people will say to that smoke: "This is a painful punishment." And it was said: it is an announcement of the imminence of the matter, as you say: "This is winter, so prepare for it."

Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 13–14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How will they have the reminder?﴾ That is, from where would they have remembrance (tadhakkur) and admonition (i'tiaz) when the punishment descends?

"And there had already come to them a clear Messenger" who makes the truth clear to them. The words dhikra (reminder) and dhikr (remembrance) are one and the same; this was stated by al-Bukhari.

"Then they turned away from him": that is, they turned away.

Ibn 'Abbas said: That is, when will they take heed, while Allah has placed them far from admonition and remembrance after their turning away from Muhammad (ﷺ) and their denial of him.

It is also said: That is, how will their saying "We are believers" benefit them after the punishment appears tomorrow, or after the signs of the Hour appear? At that point the knowledge becomes necessary (ḍarūriyyah). This is when you take the smoke as the awaited sign.

"And they said: a taught one, a madman": that is, a human taught him, or the soothsayers (kahanah) and the devils taught him; then he is a madman and not a messenger.

**Al-Qurtubi's Commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 44, verse 15:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little.﴾ That is, for a short time. He promised that He would remove that punishment from them for a little while, meaning in a brief period, so that He would know that they do not keep their word, but return to disbelief after its removal. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. When that punishment was removed from them through the prayer for rain (istisqa') of the Prophet (ﷺ), they returned to denying him.

As for the one who said that the smoke is yet to come, he said: by this he pointed to the interval that occurs between one of the signs of the Hour and another. Then whoever has been decreed to disbelief continues in his disbelief. And whoever said this refers to the Day of Resurrection said: that is, if We remove the punishment from you, you would return to disbelief. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿Indeed, you are returning﴾ is returning to Us, that is, being resurrected after death. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿Indeed, you are returning﴾ is returning to the Fire of Hell if you do not believe.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 16:

"Yawma" (on the day) is governed by what is indicated by "muntaqimun" (those who take vengeance): that is, "We will take vengeance upon them on the day We seize them (nabtishu)." Some grammarians (nahwiyyun) considered this too remote, on the ground that what comes after "inna" (indeed) does not explain what comes before it. It was also said that the governing element is "muntaqimun," but this is likewise remote, because what follows "inna" does not govern what precedes it. It is not appropriate for it to be linked to "ta'udun" (you will return) or to "inna kashifu al-'adhab" (indeed We will remove the punishment), since the meaning does not lie in that. It is permissible to put it in the accusative by supposing a verb, as if he had said: "Remind them," or "Remember." It is also permissible that the meaning is: "Indeed you will return; so when you return, I will take vengeance upon you on the day We seize with the greatest seizing." For this reason the verse is connected to the story of Pharaoh, for they promised Musa faith if he removed the punishment from them, and then they did not believe until they drowned. It was also said that "Inna kashifu al-'adhabi qalilan innakum 'a'idun" (Indeed We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return) is a complete statement, and then he begins: "Yawma nabtishu al-batshata al-kubra, inna muntaqimun" (On the day We seize with the greatest seizing, indeed We will take vengeance), meaning We will take vengeance upon all the disbelievers. It was also said that the meaning is: "Wartaqib al-dukhan, wartaqib yawma nabtishu" (Then await the smoke, and await the day We seize), where the conjunction waw has been omitted, as you say: "Beware the Fire, beware the punishment."

As for "al-batshata al-kubra" (the greatest seizing), in the view of Ibn Mas'ud it is the Day of Badr. This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mujahid and al-Dahhak. It was also said that it is the punishment of Hell on the Day of Resurrection, as stated by al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and also Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Zajjaj chose this view. It was also said that it is a smoke that occurs in this world, or hunger or famine that occurs before the Day of Resurrection. Al-Mawardi said: It is possible that it refers to the establishment of the Hour, because it is the final seizing of His in this world.

It is said: "Allah took vengeance upon him (intaqama Allahu minhu)," meaning He punished him. The noun from it is "niqmah" (vengeance), and its plural is "niqamat." It was also said that there is a distinction between "niqmah" and "'uqubah" (punishment): "'uqubah" comes after disobedience, since it derives from "'aqibah" (consequence), whereas "niqmah" may come before it, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: "'Uqubah" is that which is measured out, while "intiqam" (vengeance) is not measured.

Meaning: We tested them, i.e., We dealt with them as one who tests, by sending Musa (Moses) to them, but they denied and were destroyed. So will I do to your enemies, O Muhammad, if they do not believe. It is also said: "We tested them" means "We punished them by drowning." In the speech there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the sense is: "And there came to the people of Pharaoh a noble messenger, and We tested them," meaning, We drowned them, because the trial came after the coming of the messengers. And the conjunction waw does not indicate sequence. The meaning of "noble" (karim) is noble among his people. It is also said: noble in character through forgiveness and pardon. Al-Farra' said: noble with his Lord, since He singled him out with prophethood and with hearing speech.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning is, "He came to them and said: Follow me." So "ʿibād Allāh" ("servants of Allah") is in the vocative (munādā, a noun directly addressed). Mujahid said: The meaning is, "Send with me the servants of Allah and release them from the punishment." So "ʿibād Allāh," according to this view, is the object (maf'ūl, the direct object of the verb). It was also said: The meaning is, "Give ear to me, so that I may convey to you the message of my Lord." "Indi lakum rasūlun amīn" ("Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger"): meaning, trustworthy regarding the revelation, so accept my counsel. It was also said: trustworthy regarding what I ask of you, so I will not betray you in it. "Wa an lā taʿlū ʿalā Allāh" ("and that you not exalt yourselves against Allah"): meaning, do not be arrogant toward Him and do not rise above obedience to Him. Qatadah said: "Do not transgress against Allah." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not fabricate lies against Allah." The difference between transgression (baghy) and fabrication (iftirāʾ) is that transgression is by deed and fabrication is by speech. Ibn Jurayj said: "Do not magnify yourselves against Allah." Yahya ibn Sallam said: "Do not be proud toward the worship of Allah." The difference between magnifying oneself (taʿẓīm) and arrogance (istikbār) is that taʿẓīm is the overbearing of one who is capable, while istikbār is the haughtiness of one who is despised; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. ﴿Indi ātīkum bi-sulṭānin mubīn﴾ ("Indeed I come to you with a clear authority"). Qatadah said: "With a clear excuse." Yahya ibn Sallam said: "With a clear proof." The meaning is one: a manifest demonstration.

Qatadah said: "With a clear excuse." Yahya ibn Sallam said: "With a clear proof." The meaning is one: a manifest demonstration.

As if they had threatened him with death, so he sought refuge in God. Qatadah said: "tarjumun" means you will stone me. Ibn Abbas said: you will revile me, so that you say, "He is a sorcerer, a liar." Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Asim and Ya'qub pronounced the dhal of "udtu" distinctly (izhar), while the rest assimilated it (idgham). Idgham is preferred for the sake of lightness, and izhar is according to the original form. Then it was said: "Indeed I sought refuge in God previously, because God promised him, so He said: ﴿So they shall not reach you both﴾ [Al-Qasas: 35]. It was also said: "Inni a'udhu" (I seek refuge), just as you say, "I beseech you by God" (nashadtuka billah) and "I adjure you by God" (uqsimtu alayka billah), meaning, I swear.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 21:

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And if you do not believe me﴾, meaning: if you do not affirm me and do not believe in God on account of my proof, then the lam in "lī" (for me) is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajl, the lam expressing cause or purpose). It has also been said: meaning, "And if you do not believe in me," as in His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [[Qur'an 29:26.]] [al-Ankabut: 26], meaning, believed in him. "So leave me alone" means: let me be, sparing (kafafan) [[Meaning: your polytheism is restrained from me.]], neither for you nor against you, as Muqatil said. It has also been said: meaning, keep away from me and I will keep away from you until God judges between us. It has also been said: meaning, let my path be free and refrain from harming me. The meanings are close, and God knows best.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 44, verse 22:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he called upon his Lord﴾. In it there is an omission (ḥadhf), meaning: "So they disbelieved, and he called upon his Lord." "That these are" with the "an" (that) vowelled with a fatḥah, meaning: "that these are." "A people who are criminals" (qawmun mujrimūn), meaning: polytheists, who have refused to release the Children of Israel and [refused] faith.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 23:

There are two issues in this.

The first concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So set out with My servants by night﴾. That is, We answered his supplication and revealed to him that he should set out with My servants, meaning those among the Children of Israel who believed in Allah. ﴿By night﴾ means before morning. ﴿Indeed, you will be pursued﴾. The people of the Hijaz read ﴿فَاسْرِ﴾ (fasri) with a connected alif, as did Ibn Kathir, from sara (to travel by night). The rest read ﴿فَأَسْرِ﴾ (fa-asri) with a hamza, from asra (to travel by night). This has already been discussed [see vol. 9, p. 79]. The going out of Pharaoh after Musa, his drowning, and the deliverance of Musa have already been mentioned in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf, Ta-Ha, al-Shu'ara' and Yunus [see vol. 1, p. 389 ff.; vol. 8, p. 377 ff.; vol. 11, p. 227 ff.; vol. 13, p. 105 ff.], so there is no point in repeating it.

The second issue: Musa, peace be upon him, was commanded to depart by night. Travel at night is generally undertaken out of fear, and fear is of two kinds. Either it is fear of an enemy, in which case the night serves as a drawn curtain, and it is among the veils of Allah, the Exalted. Or it is fear of hardship upon the animals and bodies from heat or drought, in which case night travel is adopted as a benefit against that. The Prophet ﷺ used to travel by night (yasri), and go at the start of the night (yudlij), and proceed gently (yatarafaq) or hastily (yasta'jil), according to need and what the public interest requires. [Note: "yasri" means he travelled for most of the night; "yudlij" means he set out at the beginning of the night, and it is sometimes used for travel in the last part of the night.]

In the Sahih, the Prophet ﷺ said: "When you travel in fertile times, give the camels their share of the land; and when you travel in a year of drought, hasten with them to their marrow." [Note: "in the year of drought" means in a time of famine and the absence of plant growth from the land's dryness. "Al-naqy" (with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the qaf) is the marrow; the meaning is: hasten the camels in travel so that you reach the destination while they still have some strength left.] This was already discussed at the beginning of al-Nahl [see vol. 10, p. 73], and praise be to Allah.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "rahwan" means a path (ṭarīqan). Kaʿb and al-Hasan said the same. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it means a manner or bearing (samtan). al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Rabiʿ said: easy (sahlan). ʿIkrimah said: dry (yabasan), based on His saying: ﴿So strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾. It was also said: divided (muftariqan). Mujahid said: opened wide (munfarijan). It is also reported from him: dry (yabisan). It is also reported from him: still (sakinan), which is the well-known meaning in the Arabic language. Qatadah and al-Harawi said the same. Others said: opened wide (munfarijan). Ibn ʿArafah said: both of these return to one meaning, even though their wording differs, because when its flow becomes still it opens up. Likewise, the sea's flow became still and it parted for Musa, peace be upon him.

In the usage of the Arabs, rahw means still, as in the saying: "The horses came rahwan," meaning calmly still. The poet said:

*And the horses, with their bridles, gallop rahwan / like birds escaping the heavy-dropping cloud.* [[The verse is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani. "Tamzaʿ": running swiftly. This word appears corrupted in the sources: in some copies it is "tamraḥ" with rāʾ and ḥāʾ, and in others "tamraʿ" with rāʾ and ʿayn. It is also narrated as "gharban" in place of "rahwan," meaning intensity. "Al-shuʾbūb": a great cloud pouring rain.]]

al-Jawhari said: it is said, "Do that rahwan," meaning calmly, at your ease. ʿAyshun rāhin means a tranquil, comfortable life. Khimsun rāhin means easy going. Rahā al-baḥr means the sea became still. Abu ʿUbayd said: rahā between his legs, yarhū rahwan, meaning he opened them wide, and from this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And leave the sea rahwan﴾. Rahw also means easy travel; it is said, "The horses came rahwan." Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: rahā yarhū in travel means he went gently. al-Qaṭāmi said, describing riding camels:

*They walk rahwan, so the rears are not left weak, / nor do the chests rely upon the rears.*

Rahw and rahwah mean an elevated place, and also a low place where water gathers; it is among the words with opposite meanings. Abu ʿUbayd said: rahw is a hollow in the dwelling-place of a people where rainwater and other water flows. In a hadith it is reported that he ruled that (there is no pre-emption in a courtyard, nor a path, nor a *manqabah*, nor a *rukh*, nor a *rahw*) [[al-Fanāʾ: the courtyard of a house, that which extends alongside it. Al-manqabah: the path between two houses. It was also said: the path that runs over the high ground. Al-rukh (with a ḍammah): the side of the house behind it, sometimes an open space with no building.]]. Its plural is *rihāʾ*. Rahw also means a woman with a wide hip, reported by al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl. Rahw is also a kind of bird, and it is said to be the crane. al-Harawi said: it is possible that "rahwan" is an attribute of Musa (this was also said by al-Qushayri), meaning: go calmly at your ease; so rahw is an attribute of Musa and his people, not of the sea. According to the first view, it is an attribute of the sea, meaning: leave it still, as it is, parted, and do not order it to close until Pharaoh and his people enter. Qatadah said: Musa wanted to strike the sea with his staff after crossing it so that it would come together again, and he feared that Pharaoh would follow him, so this was said to him. It was also said: rahw is not from stillness but from a gap between two things; it is said, "rahā mā bayna al-rijlayn," meaning what is between the two legs was opened. So His saying "rahwan" means opened wide. al-Layth said: rahw is walking in calm; it is said, "rahā yarhū rahwan, fa-huwa rāhin." "ʿAyshun rāhin": a peaceful, prosperous life. "Ifʿal dhālika sahwan rahwan," meaning calmly, without haste. We have mentioned this already above.

﴿Indeed they﴾, meaning Pharaoh and his people, ﴿are an army to be drowned﴾. Musa was informed of this so that his heart would be at peace.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 25–27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind, and crops and a noble station﴾. "Kam" (how many) is for multiplicity. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already passed in "al-Shu'ara'" in full [[See vol. 13, p. 102 and what follows.]]. "And a delight in which they had been well-pleased (fakihin)." The ni'mah (with a fatha on the nun) is tan'im (luxury, comfort). It is said: Allah na''amahu and na'amahu, so he became comfortable (tana''ama). A woman is mu'annamah and mu'ana-mah, with the same meaning. The ni'mah (with a kasra on the nun) is a hand (favour), a benefaction, a kindness, and that which Allah has bestowed upon you. Likewise nu'ma. If you put a fatha on the nun and lengthen it, you say: al-na'ma'. And al-na'im is like it. "So-and-so has wide ni'mah," meaning he has abundant wealth; all of this is from al-Jawhari. Ibn Umar said: the intended meaning of ni'mah is the Nile of Egypt. Ibn Lahi'ah: al-Fayyum. Ibn Ziyad: the land of Egypt because of its abundant goodness. It was said: it is what they had of abundance and ease. It may be said: ni'mah and na'mah (with a kasra or fatha on the nun), related by al-Mawardi. He said: regarding the distinction between them there are two views. One: it is with a kasra on the nun for sovereignty, and with a fatha for body and religion; this was said by al-Nadr ibn Shumayl. The second: with a kasra it is from al-minnah, which is bounty and gift, and with a fatha it is from al-tan'im, which is ease of life and comfort; this was said by Ibn Ziyad.

I say: this distinction is the one found in the Sihah, and we have mentioned it. Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Abu al-Ashhab, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read "fakihin" without an alif, and its meaning is joyful and exultant. Al-Jawhari said: fakiha al-rajul (with a kasra) is fakih when he is good-natured and jocular. Al-fakih also means the exultant and the insolent. It was read "wa-ni'matin kanu fiha fakihin," meaning joyful and exultant. And "fakihin" means luxuriating. Al-Qushayri: "fakihin" means heedless and joking; it is said: he is indeed fakih, meaning a jester, and there is fukahah in him, meaning jest. Al-Tha'labi: they are two dialects, like al-hadhir and al-hadhir, and al-fari and al-farih. It was also said: al-fakih is one who enjoys all kinds of pleasure, just as the eater enjoys all kinds of fruit. And al-fakihah is what is surplus to the staple food that is indispensable.

al-Zajjaj said: That is, the matter is so, and so one stops at "kadhalika" (thus). ﴿And We caused other people to inherit them﴾ — meaning the Children of Israel. A parallel to this is ﴿And We made the people who had been oppressed inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ [al-A'raf: 137]. [Al-A'raf: 137] The verse...

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them﴾, that is, for their disbelief. "And they were not given respite" means they were not delayed from being drowned. The Arabs used to say at the death of a chief among them: "The heaven and the earth wept for him," meaning his calamity affected all things, so that the heaven, the earth, the wind and the lightning wept for him, and the wintry nights wept for him. The poet said: "The wind weeps for its grief... and the lightning flashes in the cloud" [[The verse is by Yazid ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari. It appears corrupted in the manuscripts; the correction is from Wafayat al-A'yan and Sharh al-Kamil.]]

And another said: [[He is Jarir.]]

"The sun is rising and it is not eclipsed, weeping over you for the stars of the night and the moon."

And the Khariji woman (al-Kharijiyya) said: [[al-Kharijiyya is Layla bint Tarif al-Shaybani, lamenting her brother al-Walid ibn Tarif, who was the head of the Kharijites and the most fierce of them in valour.]]

"O tree of al-Khabur, why are you in leaf, as though you did not grieve for the son of Tarif?"

All of this is by way of figurative and imaginative expression, exaggerating the obligation of grief and weeping for him. The meaning is that they perished and their loss was not great, and no one was found to mourn them. It was also said: there is an ellipsis in the statement, meaning the people of the heavens and the earth among the angels did not weep for them, as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾[[See vol. 9, p. 425.]] [Yusuf: 82]. Rather, they rejoiced at their destruction; this was said by al-Hasan. Yazid al-Raqqashi related from Anas ibn Malik who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is not a believer except that he has two doors in the heaven: a door from which his provision descends and a door through which his speech and his deeds ascend. When he dies, the two of them lose him and weep for him." Then he recited: "So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them." This means that they did not do a righteous deed on earth for which it would weep over them, nor did any righteous deed ascend for them to the heaven, so that it would weep at the loss of that.

Mujahid said: The heaven and the earth weep over the believer for forty mornings. Abu Yahya said: "I was amazed at his saying, so he said: Are you amazed? And why should the earth not weep for a servant who populates it with bowing and prostration? And why should the heaven not weep for a servant whose glorifying and magnifying of Him in it was like the humming of bees!" Ali and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: His place of prayer on earth weeps for him, and the ascent of his deeds from the heaven. The meaning of the verse according to this is: "So the ascending places of their deeds from the heaven did not weep for them, nor the places of their worship from the earth." This is also the meaning of the statement of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

As for the weeping of the heaven and the earth, there are three interpretations. The first is that it is like the known weeping of living beings, and this is probably the view of Mujahid. Shurayh al-Hadrami said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Islam began as something strange and it will return to being strange as it began, so good tidings to the strangers on the Day of Resurrection." It was said: "Who are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "They are those who put things right when people have corrupted." Then he said: "Indeed there is no strangeness for a believer, and no believer dies in a foreign land, absent from those who weep for him, except that the heaven and the earth weep for him." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them." Then he said: "Indeed, the two do not weep for the disbeliever."

I say: Abu Nu'aym Muhammad ibn Ma'mar [[In (n z): Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz said: Muhammad ibn Ma'mar narrated to us...]] said: Abu Shu'ayb al-Harrani narrated to us, who said: Yahya ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, who said: al-Awza'i narrated to us, who said: Ata al-Khurasani narrated to me, who said: There is no servant who prostrates to Allah in a spot on the earth except that it bears witness for him on the Day of Resurrection, and weeps for him on the day he dies.

It was also said: their weeping is the redness of their horizons. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and by Ata, al-Suddi, and al-Tirmidhi (Muhammad ibn Ali), and it was related from al-Hasan. Al-Suddi said: When al-Husayn ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, was killed, the heaven wept for him, and its weeping was its redness. Jarir related from Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad who said: When al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, was killed, the horizons of the heaven turned red for him for four months. Yazid said: Its reddening is its weeping. Muhammad ibn Sirin said: They told us that the redness that occurs with the twilight (shafaq) did not exist until al-Husayn ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, was killed. Sulayman al-Qadi said: "We were rained upon with blood on the day al-Husayn was killed."

I say: al-Daraqutni related, from the hadith of Malik ibn Anas, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The twilight (ash-shafaq) is the redness." And from Ubada ibn al-Samit and Shaddad ibn Aws, who both said: "The twilight is of two kinds: the redness and the whiteness; when the redness sets, the prayer becomes permissible." And from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The twilight is the redness." This refutes what Ibn Sirin related. It has already been mentioned in "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 220.]] from Qurrah ibn Khalid who said: The heaven did not weep for anyone except Yahya ibn Zakariyya and al-Husayn ibn Ali, and its redness is its weeping.

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: Weeping is the outpouring of a thing. When the eye pours out its water, it is said to have wept; when the heaven pours out its redness, it is said to have wept; and when the earth pours out its dustiness, it is said to have wept. This is because the believer is a light, and with him is the light of Allah, so the earth is illuminated by his light even though he is absent from your eyes. If it loses the light of the believer, it becomes dusty and pours out in its dustiness, because it was dusty with the sins of the people of polytheism, and it only became illuminated by the light of the believer. So when the believer is taken from it, it pours out with its dustiness.

Anas said: On the day the Prophet (ﷺ) entered Medina, everything was illuminated. On the day he passed away, everything became dark, and while we were in his burial we did not shake our hands of the dust until we denied our hearts. As for the weeping of the heaven, its redness is as al-Hasan said.

Nasr ibn Asim said: The first of the signs is a redness that appears, and that is only for the approach of the Hour, so it pours out with weeping because it is empty of the lights of the believers. It was also said: its weeping is a sign that appears from it, indicating sorrow and grief.

I say: The first view is the most apparent, since there is no impossibility in that. And since the heavens and the earth glorify, hear and speak, as we have explained in "Subhan," "Maryam," and "Ha Mim Fussilat" [[See vol. 10, p. 266; vol. 11, p. 157; vol. 15, p. 344]], so they weep likewise, along with what has come in the report about that. And Allah knows best the correctness of these views. [[What is between the brackets is an addition from (n).]]

Qurtubi's commentary on verses 30–31 of Surah al-Dukhan.

That is, what the Copts used to do to them by Pharaoh's command: killing their sons, keeping their women alive for service, enslaving them, and imposing on them arduous labours.

"Min Fir'awn" (from Pharaoh) is a substitute (badal) for "al-'adhab al-muhin" (the humiliating torment), so "min" is not connected to the word "min" in "min al-'adhab" (from the torment), because the noun has already been described, and a word does not function as a verb after its description has been given. It has also been said: the meaning is "We delivered them from the torment and from Pharaoh."

"Innahu kana 'aliyan mina al-musrifin" (Indeed he was haughty, among the transgressors): that is, a tyrant among the polytheists. This loftiness is not one of praise; rather it is loftiness in transgression, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [[Verse 4 of Surah al-Qasas.]] [al-Qasas: 4]. It has also been said: this loftiness is his exalting himself above worshipping God.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 32:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We chose them﴾, meaning the Children of Israel. "Upon knowledge" means: upon knowledge from Us of them, because of the great number of prophets among them. "Above the worlds" means: above the worlds of their own time, as evidenced by His saying to this Ummah: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾[[Verse 11, Surah Al 'Imran.]] [Al 'Imran: 110]. This is the view of Qatadah and others. It has also been said: "above all the worlds" by virtue of the prophets placed among them. This (preference) was exclusive to them and not to others; this is related by Ibn 'Isa, al-Zamakhshari and others. And His saying "You were the best nation" would then mean: after the Children of Israel. And Allah knows best. It has also been said: this choosing refers to their deliverance from drowning and their being made heirs to the land after Pharaoh.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verses 34–36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, these people are saying﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh: "There is nothing but our first death" (al-ibtida' wa-l-khabar, a subject and predicate construction), like ﴿There is nothing but your trial﴾[[Verse 155, Surah al-A'raf.]] [al-A'raf: 155], and ﴿There is nothing but our worldly life﴾[[Verse 29, Surah al-An'am.]] [al-Mu'minun: 37]. "And we will not be resurrected" (mun-shareen), meaning, will not be raised up (mab'uthin). "So bring our fathers, if you are truthful." Allah resurrects the dead, and they are resurrected. It was also said: the first of them was named Tubba' because he followed the horn of the sun and travelled in the East with the armies.

It is also permissible that "from before them" be the relative clause of "those," and the adverbial complement returns to the relative pronoun. In that case, "We destroyed them" has one of two readings: either "qad" is to be understood with it, so that it is in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal); or an omitted qualified noun is to be understood, as if he said: a people We destroyed. It is also permissible that "those" be in the genitive place, conjoined to "Tubba'," as if he said: the people of Tubba', the destroyers before them. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verses 41–42:**

Allah's words: ﴿On the Day when no protector will avail a protector in anything﴾. "Yawma" is a substitution (*badal*) for the first "yawma."

*Mawla* means a *wali* (close kinsman or helper), and it is the cousin (*ibn al-amm*) and the helper. The meaning is that a cousin does not ward off [punishment] from his cousin, nor a relative from his relative, nor a friend from his friend. "Wa la hum yunsarun" means that a believer does not help an unbeliever because of kinship. A parallel to this verse is ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], and so on.

Or it is in the nominative as a beginning (*mubtada'*), with the predicate (*khabar*) omitted, as if he said: "Except whom Allah has mercy upon, he is forgiven," or "he will avail him, intercede, and help." Or it is a substitution from the first "mawla," as if he said: "No one avails except whom Allah has mercy upon." According to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', it is in the accusative case (*nasb*) as a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: "But whoever Allah has mercy upon, the things for which they need someone among the created beings to avail them will not reach them." It is also permissible for it to be a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), meaning: no relative avails a relative except the believers, for they are permitted to intercede for one another.

"Innahu huwa al-'Aziz al-Rahim" means: He is the One who takes vengeance on His enemies and is merciful to His friends (*awliya'*), as He said: ﴿Severe in punishment, Owner of bounty﴾ [Ghafir: 3]. Thus He combined the promise with the threat.

He and Ibn Mas'ud recited it this way. Hammam ibn al-Harith said: Abu al-Darda' was teaching a man, "Indeed, the tree of zaqqum is the food of the sinner" (طَعَامُ الْأَثِيمِ), but the man kept saying "food of the orphan" (طَعَامُ الْيَتِيمِ). When he did not understand, [Abu al-Darda'] said to him: "Food of the wicked" (طَعَامُ الْفَاجِرِ). Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: My father narrated to me, saying: Nasr narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Ubayd narrated to us, saying: Nu'aym ibn Hammad narrated to us, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Muhammad, from Ibn 'Ajlan, from 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ud, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud taught a man, "Indeed, the tree of zaqqum. When 'Abd Allah saw that the man's tongue would not go straight with the correct reading, he said to him: "Can you not say 'food of the wicked' (طَعَامُ الْفَاجِرِ)?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then do so."

There is no proof in this for the ignorant among the people of deviation (أَهْلِ الزَّيْغِ) that it is permissible to replace a letter of the Qur'an with another. This was only from 'Abd Allah, as a way of bringing the learner closer, and as a preparation for him to return to the correct reading, while maintaining the truth and speaking the letter as it was sent down by God and as related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "By this it is inferred that substituting one word for another word is permissible when it conveys its meaning. From this, Abu Hanifah (رحمه الله) permitted recitation in Persian on a condition, namely that the reciter conveys the meanings in their entirety without omitting any of them. They said: This condition testifies that it is a permission that is not a permission, because in the speech of the Arabs, especially in the Qur'an, which is miraculous in its eloquence, the strangeness of its composition and its styles, there are subtle meanings and purposes that no tongue, whether Persian or otherwise, can independently convey. Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, did not have good command of Persian, so this was not from him based on verification and insight." 'Ali ibn al-Ja'd narrated from Abu Yusuf, from Abu Hanifah, the same as the view of his two companions in denying recitation in Persian.

The tree of zaqqum: the tree that God created in Hell and named "the cursed tree." When the people of the Fire are hungry, they seek refuge in it and eat from it, and it boils in their bellies as boiling water boils. What reaches their bellies from it is likened to al-muhl (الْمُهْلِ), which is molten copper.

The recitation of the common readers is "taghli" (تَغْلِي) with the letter ta' (بِالتَّاءِ), taking it to refer to the tree. Ibn Kathir, Hafs, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited "yaghli" (يَغْلِي) with the letter ya' (بِالْيَاءِ), taking it to refer to the food, which has the same meaning as the tree. It is not taken to refer to al-muhl, because that is mentioned as a comparison.

Al-Athim (الْأَثِيمِ) is "the one who sins" (الآثم), from athima, yaʾthimu, ithman, as said by al-Qushayri and Ibn 'Isa. It was also said that it is the polytheist who earns sin, as said by Yahya ibn Salam. The reason is that he said: "Muhammad promises us that in Hell there is zaqqum, but it is only thariad with butter and dates." So God made clear the opposite of what he had said.

Al-Naqqash related from Mujahid that the tree of zaqqum is Abu Jahl. I say: This is not authentic from Mujahid, and it is refuted by what we mentioned about this tree in surat al-Saffat and surat Subhan [[see vol. 10, p. 283 and vol. 15, p. (85)]] as well.

Ibn Kathir, Hafs, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited "yaghli" (يَغْلِي) with the letter ya' (بِالْيَاءِ), taking it to refer to the food, which has the same meaning as the tree. It is not taken to refer to al-muhl, because that is mentioned as a comparison.

Al-Athim (الْأَثِيمِ) is "the one who sins" (الآثم), from athima, yaʾthimu, ithman, as said by al-Qushayri and Ibn 'Isa. It was also said that it is the polytheist who earns sin, as said by Yahya ibn Salam. In al-Sihah (the lexicon): "The man sinned (with kasra) ithman and ma'tham when he fell into sin, so he is āthim and athim as well." So the meaning of "food of the sinner" (طَعامُ الْأَثِيمِ) is "the one possessing sin, the wicked," [[In ḥ z l: i.e., he is the sinner, the wicked.]] and that is Abu Jahl. The reason is that he said: "Muhammad promises us that in Hell there is zaqqum, but it is only thariad with butter and dates." So God made clear the opposite of what he had said.

Al-Naqqash related from Mujahid that the tree of zaqqum is Abu Jahl. I say: This is not authentic from Mujahid, and it is refuted by what we mentioned about this tree in surat al-Saffat and surat Subhan [[see vol. 10, p. 283 and vol. 15, p. (85)]] as well.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 44, verses 47–48:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Seize him﴾, meaning it is said to the Zabaniyah (the angels of punishment), "Seize him," referring to the sinner. "Then drag him" means pull him and drive him forward. Al-'Atl (dragging) is to seize a man by the collar of his garment and drag him toward you, so that you take him away to prison or to affliction. It is said: "I 'ataltu al-rajul, a'tiluhu and a'tuluhu, 'atlan," when you pull the man violently. A man is "mi'tal" (with kasra). He said, describing a horse:

*"We pull at it, pulling by the forelock, and we do not drag it."* [The speaker is Abu al-Najm, and before it is:]

*"It flew away from the foal, speeding, from the broad-shouldered one, a free mare."*

There are two dialect forms: 'atalahu and 'atanahu (with lam and with nun, both), as stated by Ibn al-Sikkit. The Kufans and Abu 'Amr read "fa-'-tiluhu" with kasra, while the rest read it with damma. ﴿To the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ means to the middle of Hell. ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of boiling water﴾. Muqatil said: Malik, the keeper of the Fire, strikes Abu Jahl on the head with an iron mace (miqma'), so that his head is shattered and his brain spills out, and it runs onto his body. Then the angel pours over him scalding water whose heat has subsided, and it falls into his belly. The angel then says: "Taste the punishment." A parallel to this is the verse ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ [al-Hajj: 19].

God Almighty says: ﴿Taste it, for you are the mighty, the noble.﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: The common readers have agreed on the kasra in "inna" (إِنَّ). It is narrated from al-Hasan, from Ali, may Allah have mercy on him, that he read "dhuq innaka" with a fatha on the "anna" (أَنَّ), and al-Kisa'i (a famous reader of the Qur'an) recited it this way. Whoever reads "inna" with a kasra pauses on "dhuq." Whoever reads it with a fatha does not pause on "dhuq," because the meaning is: taste it because you are, and that you are the mighty, the noble.

Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, who had said: "There is no one in it mightier or nobler than me." Therefore it was said to him: ﴿Taste it, for you are the mighty, the noble.﴾

Ikrimah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) met Abu Jahl, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has commanded me to say to you: 'Woe to you, and woe again.'" So he said: "With what do you threaten me? By Allah, neither you nor your Lord can do anything to me. I am among the mightiest of this valley and the most honored of its people." Then Allah killed him on the Day of Badr and humiliated him, and this verse was revealed. That is, the angel says to him: "Taste it, for you are the mighty, the noble, by your own claim."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verses 51–53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the God-conscious will be in a secure place﴾. When He mentioned the abode of the disbelievers and their punishment, He mentioned the lodging of the believers and their bliss. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "fi muqamin" with a ḍammah on the mim, and the rest read it with a fatḥah. Al-Kisa'i said: al-maqam is the place, and al-muqam is the staying (al-iqamah), as the poet said:

"The abodes were effaced, their place and their staying [[This is the opening line of the Mu'allaqah of Labid. Its completion is:

in Mina, its gazelles and their droppings have become eternal]]"

Al-Jawhari said: As for al-maqam and al-muqam, each of them may mean the staying (al-iqamah), and it may mean the place of standing. For if you derive it from qama yaqumu, it is with a fatḥah; and if you derive it from aqama yuqimu, it is with a ḍammah, because when the verb exceeds three letters, the place takes a ḍammah on the mim, since it is patterned on the quadriliteral forms, like daḥraja, and "hadha mudahrijuna." It was also said: al-maqam (with a fatḥah) is the station and the assembly, and (with a ḍammah) it may be meant as the place, and it may be a verbal noun with an omitted modifier estimated in it, i.e., in a place of staying.

"Secure" (amin): one is safe in it from calamities.

﴿In gardens and springs﴾: this is a substitute (badal) for "in a secure place."

﴿They will wear fine silk and brocade, facing one another﴾: they will not see the backs of one another; they will face each other, and their gathering will turn with them wherever they turn. Al-Sundus is what is thin of brocade (dibaj), and al-Istabraq is what is thick of it. This has already been discussed in "al-Kahf" [[See vol. 10, p. 397]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 44, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning: the matter is so, as we have mentioned. Thus one pauses at "thus." It was also said: meaning, just as We admitted them to Paradise and did with them what was mentioned earlier, thus We honored them by marrying them to ḥūr ʿīn (wide-eyed maidens). The discussion of ʿīn has already passed in "al-Ṣāffāt" [[See vol. 15, p. 4]]. The ḥūr (sing. ḥawrāʾ), according to Qatadah and the majority, are the white ones: the ḥawrāʾ is the fair woman whose shin can be seen through her garments, and the beholder can see his face in her ankle, like a mirror, due to the thinness of the skin, the softness of the complexion and the clarity of the color. The evidence for this interpretation is that in the reading of Ibn Masʿud it is ﴿bi-ʿīsin ʿīn﴾ [[al-ʿīs (with kasra): whiteness mixed with a little reddish tint.]]. Abu Bakr al-Anbari reported: Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn told us, saying: Ḥusayn told us, saying: ʿAmmar ibn Muhammad told us, saying: I prayed behind Mansur ibn al-Muʿtamir, and he recited in "Ḥā Mīm" (al-Dukhan): ﴿bi-ʿīsin ʿīn. Lā yadhūqūna fīhā al-mawta illā al-mawtata al-ūlā﴾. Al-ʿīs means the white ones, and from this the white camels are called ʿīs; its singular is baʿīr aʿyas and female camel ʿayyāʾ. Imru al-Qays said:

They incline toward my voice when they hear it, as the young she-camels (ʿayṭ) incline toward the voice of a white-hued camel [[al-ʿayṭ (plural of ʿayṭāʾ): a young female camel that has not borne young.]].

So the meaning of ḥūr here is: beautiful ones, intensely white with beauty. Ibn al-Mubarak reported: Maʿmar told us, from Abu Ishaq, from ʿAmr ibn Maymun al-Awdi, from Ibn Masʿud, who said: Indeed, a woman among the ḥūr ʿīn, the marrow of her shin can be seen from behind the flesh and bone, and from beneath seventy garments, as red drink is seen in a white glass. Mujahid said: The ḥūr were so named because the gaze is dazzled by their beauty, their whiteness and the clarity of their color. It was also said: they were called ḥūr because of the ḥawar of their eyes, and ḥawar is the intense whiteness of the eye with intense blackness. One says: a woman ḥawrāʾ, clearly ḥawar. It is said: his eye became ḥawarr (reddened/whitened), iḥwirrāran; and the thing ḥawarra meant it became white. Al-Asmaʿi said: I do not know what ḥawar in eyes is. Abu ʿAmr said: ḥawar is that the whole eye becomes black, like the eyes of gazelles and cows. He said: there is no ḥawar among the sons of Adam; women were called ḥūr al-ʿīn only because they are likened to gazelles and cows. Al-ʿAjjaj said:

With eyes made ḥawwarāt, ḥūr [[In the originals: "with eyes made white" (bi-ʿuyūnin muḥawwarātin bīḍin); the correction is from the Arjuza of al-ʿAjjaj. Its line is: "when they peer through the gaps of the curtains," and after it: "sidelong-glancing at the door toward the ṣūr."]]

meaning the eyes that are pure in whiteness, intensely black in the pupils. ʿīn is the plural of ʿaynāʾ, the one with wide, large eyes. From Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (The bridal gifts (mahr) of the ḥūr ʿīn are handfuls of dates and pieces of bread). And from Abu Qirṣafah [[Abu Qirṣafah (with the first letter kasra): his name is Jundarah ibn Khaythanah al-Kinani.]] who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: (Removing the rubbish from the mosque is the mahr of the ḥūr ʿīn). And from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: (Sweeping the mosques is the mahr of the ḥūr ʿīn), mentioned by al-Tha'labi, may Allah have mercy on him. We have devoted a separate chapter to this meaning in (Kitab al-Tadhkirah), and praise be to Allah. It is disputed which is better in Paradise: the women of the children of Adam or the ḥūr? Ibn al-Mubarak reported: He said: Rushdin told us, from Ibn Anʿum, from Ḥibban ibn Abi Jabalah, who said: Indeed, the women of the children of Adam who enter Paradise from among them are preferred over the ḥūr ʿīn because of what they did in this world. It has been narrated with a marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet) report that (the women of the children of Adam are better than the ḥūr ʿīn by seventy thousand times). It was also said: the ḥūr ʿīn are better, based on his peace be upon him saying in his supplication: (And replace him with a spouse better than his spouse). And Allah knows best. Qarʾa ʿIkrimah ﴿bi-ḥūrin ʿīn﴾ with an idafah (construct). The idafah and the tanwin in ﴿bi-ḥūrin ʿīnin﴾ are equivalent.

Qatadah said: "Secure" (āminīn) from death, from weariness (al-waṣab), and from Satan. It was also said: secure from the cessation of the delight they are in, or from any harm or disliked thing reaching them from eating of it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 44, verses 56–57:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾. That is, they will absolutely not taste death in it, because they are abiding in it. Then He said, ﴿except the first death﴾ as a discontinuous exception (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: but the first death, they have already tasted it in this world. Sibawayh recited:

Whoever was the swiftest in the scattering of Falij,
then its she-camels were mangy together and dispersed.

Then he made an exception with something that is not of the first kind, saying:

Except like the shoot which you wasted,
like a branch in its tender growth, flourishing.

It has been said that *illa* (except) here means *ba'da* (after), as in your saying: "I have not spoken to a man today except a man with you," meaning after a man with you. It has also been said that *illa* means *siwa* (other than), that is, other than the death they died in the world, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [An-Nisa: 22]. This is like your saying: "I have not tasted food today other than what I ate yesterday."

Al-Qutabi said: The meaning of ﴿except the first death﴾ is that when the believer approaches death, the angels of mercy receive him and he meets rest and fragrance (*al-rawh wa al-rayhan*). His death is in Paradise because he is characterized by its causes. So this is a genuine exception. Death is an accident that cannot be tasted, but it has been made like food whose taste is disliked, so the word "taste" is used for it metaphorically.

﴿And He protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire, as a bounty from your Lord﴾. That is, He did this for them out of His grace toward them. "Bounty" (*fadlan*) is a verbal noun governed by "they call" (*yad'una*). It has been said that its governing verb is "and He protected them." It has also been said that it is a hidden verb. It has been said that the meaning is according to the preceding statement, since it is a favour from Him to them, as He guided them in the world to deeds by which they enter Paradise.

﴿That is the great achievement﴾, that is, the happiness, the great gain, and the great salvation. It has been said that it derives from your saying "faza bi-kadha," meaning he obtained it and gained it.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 44, verses 58–59:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We have made it easy in your tongue﴾, meaning the Qur'an, that is, We made it easy for you and for whoever recites it, by your language.

﴿So that they may remember﴾, that is, that they may take heed and be restrained. A parallel to this is ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ [Al-Qamar 54:17, 22, 32, 40] [[Verses 17, 22, 32 and 40 of Surah al-Qamar.]] [Al-Qamar 54:17]. Thus He concluded the surah by urging the following of the Qur'an, even though it was not mentioned, just as He said at the opening of the surah: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ [Al-Dukhan 44:3] [[See vol. 20, p.]], ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [Al-Qadr 97:1], as has preceded.

﴿So wait, [Muhammad], indeed they are waiting﴾, that is, wait for what I have promised you of victory over them, [for] they are awaiting your death; this is related by al-Naqqash. It has also been said: wait for the victory from your Lord, [for] they are awaiting, in their own assumption, your defeat. It has also been said: wait for Allah to judge between you and them, for they are awaiting for you the misfortunes of time (rayb al-hadathan). The meanings are close. It has also been said: wait for the reward I have promised you, for they are like those awaiting the punishment I have promised them. It has also been said: wait for the Day of Resurrection, for it is the Day of Judgment, and even though they do not believe in the occurrence of the Resurrection, they are treated as those who await it, because their end is that (Day). And Allah Exalted knows best.

﴿So that they may remember﴾, that is, that they may take heed and be restrained. A parallel to this is ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ [Al-Qamar 54:17, 22, 32, 40] [[Verses 17, 22, 32 and 40 of Surah al-Qamar.]] [Al-Qamar 54:17]. Thus He concluded the surah by urging the following of the Qur'an, even though it was not mentioned, just as He said at the opening of the surah: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ [Al-Dukhan 44:3] [[See vol. 20, p.]], ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [Al-Qadr 97:1], as has preceded.

﴿So wait, [Muhammad], indeed they are waiting﴾, that is, wait for what I have promised you of victory over them, [for] they are awaiting your death; this is related by al-Naqqash. It has also been said: wait for the victory from your Lord, [for] they are awaiting, in their own assumption, your defeat. It has also been said: wait for Allah to judge between you and them, for they are awaiting for you the misfortunes of time (rayb al-hadathan). The meanings are close. It has also been said: wait for the reward I have promised you, for they are like those awaiting the punishment I have promised them. It has also been said: wait for the Day of Resurrection, for it is the Day of Judgment, and even though they do not believe in the occurrence of the Resurrection, they are treated as those who await it, because their end is that (Day). And Allah Exalted knows best.
